title: Big-O in plain words
summary: How to describe the way code slows down as data grows, the five growth rates you will meet most, and how to spot a hidden slow loop in code Claude writes.
youWillLearn: The five common growth rates, from O(1) to O(n²), with real numbers
How to trade a little memory for a lot of speed
How to spot hidden loops like .includes() inside .map()

glossary.Big-O: A short way to describe how the work a piece of code does grows as its input grows, ignoring small details.
glossary.n: The size of the input: how many notes, tags, characters or rows the code has to handle.
glossary.time complexity: How the number of steps grows with n. Written in Big-O, like O(n).
glossary.space complexity: How the extra memory the code needs grows with n. Also written in Big-O.
glossary.constant time: The work stays the same no matter how big n gets. Written O(1).
glossary.linear time: The work grows in step with n: twice the notes, twice the work. Written O(n).
glossary.quadratic time: The work grows with n times n, usually from a loop inside a loop. Written O(n²).
glossary.logarithmic time: The work grows very slowly because each step cuts the problem in half. Written O(log n).
glossary.Set: A JavaScript collection of unique values that can answer "is this in here?" in about one step.
glossary.app server: The computer that runs Notely's own code and answers every click.
glossary.timeout: A time limit. When work takes longer, the server stops it and returns an error instead.

steps.title: A duplicate finder that feels instant
body: Notely, our notes app, gets a Find duplicates button. Maya, a user, clicks it. The app server (the computer running Notely's code) loads her notes from the database, where every note is kept, and compares their titles.
Claude Code wrote the function. You test it with Maya's 10 notes: about 45 comparisons, instant.

scene.caption: Maya clicks, the app server loads her notes and compares titles.

steps.title: 100,000 notes, and it never finishes
body: Then Maya imports 100,000 notes. The same button now runs until the app server hits its timeout, the time limit after which it gives up.
Nothing is broken. The code does far more work than you expected as the data grew: about five billion comparisons. We need a way to talk about that growth.
changes: ~ App Server: stopped at its time limit

scene.caption: Same code, more notes: the app server gives up before it finishes.

steps.title: Big-O describes growth, not seconds
body: Big-O answers one question: if the input gets bigger, how much more work does the code do? The input size is called n.
A loop that touches each note once does about n steps. That is written O(n), linear time: double the notes, double the work. Machine speed does not matter, only the shape of the growth.

callout.text: Reading every page of a book to find a word takes longer for a longer book, in proportion. That is O(n). Big-O is about how the effort scales, not how fast you read.

changes: − Maya, App Server, Database: we zoom into the code
+ Linear: one loop over the notes, O(n)
~ Steps 5,000,000,000 → 100,000: now for the block in focus

scene.caption: The first rung of a ladder: one pass over n notes.

steps.title: O(1): the same work at any size
body: Some operations ignore the data's size. Reading notes[5] from a list, or looking up a key in a hash map (a lookup table, next lesson), takes one step for ten notes or ten million.
That is constant time, written O(1): the best you can get, and why hash maps show up in so many interview answers.

callout.text: You met key-value caches like Redis in system design: lookup by key is O(1) on average. Same idea, inside one function.

changes: + Constant: one step at any size, O(1)
~ Linear: no longer in focus

scene.caption: O(1) sits at the cheap end of the ladder.

steps.title: O(n²): a loop inside a loop
body: Here is the duplicate finder Claude wrote. For each note, it compares against every later note: a loop inside a loop.
With n notes that is about n × n / 2 comparisons. Big-O drops the / 2 and keeps the shape: quadratic time, O(n²). For 100,000 notes, about five billion comparisons. That was the timeout.

code.caption: n(n-1)/2 comparisons. Big-O drops the /2: it is still O(n²).

changes: + Nested loop: a loop inside a loop, O(n²)
~ Constant: no longer in focus

scene.caption: O(n²) sits at the expensive end. This is where the timeout came from.

steps.title: O(log n) and O(n log n): halving
body: Some code cuts the problem in half at each step, like opening a dictionary in the middle. 100,000 notes need only about 17 halvings: logarithmic time, O(log n).
Good sorting does about log n rounds of work over all n items: O(n log n), about 1.7 million steps here. Remember it as "the cost of sorting".
changes: + Halving: half the work is gone each step, O(log n)
+ Sorting: the cost of a good sort, O(n log n)
~ Steps 5,000,000,000 → 17 with halving
~ Nested loop: no longer in focus

scene.caption: The full ladder, from cheapest to most expensive.

steps.title: Trade memory for speed with a Set
body: Back to the duplicate finder. Walk the notes once and remember each title in a Set, a collection that answers "seen this?" in about one step.
One pass of O(1) checks: O(n) time complexity. The Set grows with the notes: O(n) extra memory, its space complexity. Five billion comparisons become 100,000.

callout.text: In an interview, always say both: "This is O(n) time and O(n) space." Interviewers often ask for both, and saying it first shows you think about the trade-off.

code.caption: O(n) time, O(n) space. Same answer, finishes in milliseconds.

changes: − Constant, Halving, Linear, Sorting, Nested loop
+ Maya, App Server, Database: back in the app
+ Seen titles: a Set of every title met so far
~ Steps 17 → 100,000, done in milliseconds

scene.caption: One pass over the notes, one quick Set check per note.

steps.title: Hidden loops hide in one-liners
body: Not every loop looks like one. .includes(), .indexOf() and .find() each scan a whole list. Say we mark Maya's pinned notes: for each of 100,000 notes, .includes() scans a list of 1,000 pinned ids. One tidy line, 100 million steps.
The same trap exists one level up: a database query inside a loop sends one query per note.

callout.text: In data-handling code, look for .includes, .find or .indexOf inside a loop or callback, and await on a query inside for. Ask: "What is the time complexity of this, and how big can n get in production?"

changes: − Seen titles
+ Pinned ids: a list scanned again for every note
~ App Server: slow again

scene.caption: 100,000 notes, each checked against 1,000 pinned ids: 100 million steps.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Big-O describes how work grows with n, not how many seconds it takes. From best to worst: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²).
Nested loops, including hidden ones like .includes() in a loop, are the usual cause of slow code. A Set or Map often trades O(n) memory for a big drop in time.
changes: − Maya, App Server, Database, Pinned ids
+ Constant, Halving, Linear: the cheap rungs
+ Sorting, Nested loop: the expensive rungs

scene.caption: The Big-O ladder: aim for the left, watch out for the right.

quiz.question: A function loops over Maya's notes once, and inside the loop it calls tags.includes(note.tag) on an array of all tags. What is its time complexity, with n notes and m tags?

options.text: O(n), because there is only one visible loop.
options.why: includes() is a loop too: it scans the tags array each time, so the work multiplies.
For each of the n notes, includes() may scan all m tags. Turning tags into a Set first makes it O(n + m).

options.text: O(1), because includes() is a built-in.
options.why: Built-in does not mean free. Array methods like includes, indexOf and find scan the array.

quiz.question: Approach A takes 3n steps. Approach B takes n² steps. With n = 10,000, which statement is right?

options.text: A is O(3n), so it is three times slower than B.
options.why: Big-O drops constants: A is O(n). And at n = 10,000, B does 100 million steps while A does 30,000.

options.text: They are about the same, since both depend on n.
options.why: Depending on n is not enough. How it grows matters: linear stays manageable, quadratic explodes.

options.text: A is O(n) and B is O(n²). A wins by a wide margin at this size.
options.why: 30,000 steps against 100,000,000. The gap keeps widening as n grows.

quiz.question: Claude Code fixed a slow duplicate check by adding a Set of seen values. A reviewer says "but now it uses more memory". What is the best reply?

options.text: True: O(n) extra space, in exchange for going from O(n²) to O(n) time. For 100,000 notes that trade is clearly worth it.
options.why: Naming both the time and the space cost, and why the trade fits the data size, is exactly the reasoning interviewers look for.

options.text: Sets use no extra memory, so nothing changed.
options.why: A Set stores every value you add, so it grows with n.

options.text: Go back to the nested loop to save memory.
options.why: A few megabytes of memory is cheap. A function that times out at 100,000 notes is a broken feature.

takeaways: Big-O describes how work grows as the input grows, not how many seconds it takes.
Know the ladder: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²). Drop constants and keep the biggest term.
A loop inside a loop is O(n²). So is .includes(), .find() or .indexOf() inside a loop.
A Set or Map often trades O(n) memory for O(n) instead of O(n²) time.
Always state both: "O(n) time, O(n) space", and ask how big n gets in production.
